Sandwich Variance of the Coefficients

Source: R/sandwich.R
hc0_sandwich.Rd

Select the meat of the frequentist variance \(V = V_b B V_b\), with \(V_b = (H + S)^{-1}\) the inverse of the penalized information and \(B\) built from the scores of the observations. Pass the object as the sandwich argument of frequentist_vcov().

Usage

hc0_sandwich(cluster = NULL, data = NULL)

hc1_sandwich(cluster = NULL, data = NULL)

Arguments

cluster

NULL (the default) or a one-sided formula with a single variable of the data, such as ~ id.

data

NULL (the default) or the data frame that holds the cluster variable, with one row for each observation of the fit.

Value

A SandwichMethod object with the properties type ("HC0" or "HC1"), cluster and data.

Details

The score \(u_i\) of observation \(i\) is the derivative of its log-likelihood, with no penalty in it, in the whole vector of coefficients: the fixed coefficients and the smooth coefficients of every distribution parameter, and the random effects, which are treated as penalized coefficients. The matrix \(B\) is \(\sum_i u_i u_i'\), or \(\sum_g U_g U_g'\) with \(U_g = \sum_{i \in g} u_i\) over the clusters \(g\) when cluster is given. The estimator is therefore the robust counterpart of the frequentist variance of frequentist_vcov(), conditional on the random effects and on the hyperparameters. It does not contain the smoothing bias of a penalized term, as the frequentist variance does not.

hc0_sandwich() applies no correction (HC0, and CR0 with a cluster). hc1_sandwich() multiplies by \(n/(n - p)\) (HC1), and by \(G/(G - 1) \cdot (n - 1)/(n - p)\) with a cluster (CR1), where \(G\) is the number of clusters. A cluster for each observation reduces CR0 to HC0 and CR1 to HC1. Here \(p\) is the effective degrees of freedom of the whole model, random effects included, which is not the number of columns of the design where a term is penalized.

The cluster variable is read from data when that argument is given and from the data of the call to statmod() otherwise, which is evaluated again in the environment of the model formula. A fit does not keep its data, so the second route fails once the data frame is gone or has changed.

The meat always uses the score of the likelihood. With ml() the scores sum to zero at the fit, apart from the penalty. Under reml() a coordinate that the marginal criterion estimates, such as the scale of a Gaussian, has a likelihood score that is not zero at the fit, and the sandwich includes that offset.

A cluster must contain every group of a modelterms7::random() term entirely. With no cluster the observations are treated as independent given the random effects.

Models with a structural term (modelterms7::gas(), modelterms7::regime()), with a term whose block moves with its coefficients (the break-point terms and modelterms7::nl()) are rejected. hac_sandwich() covers the structural terms.

The prior weights \(w_i\) of statmod() are frequency weights: row \(i\) stands for \(w_i\) identical observations. Without a cluster the copies are separate observations and \(B = \sum_i w_i g_i g_i'\), with \(g_i\) the score of one copy, and \(n = \sum_i w_i\) in the HC1 factor. With a cluster the copies stay in the cluster of the row, so \(U_g = \sum_{i \in g} w_i g_i\), \(G\) is the number of clusters with positive weight and \(n = \sum_i w_i\). A row with weight zero contributes nothing and is not counted. The result equals the unweighted estimator on the data expanded to \(w_i\) copies of each row, for integer weights.

References

White, H. (1980). A heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimator and a direct test for heteroskedasticity. Econometrica, 48(4), 817–838.

MacKinnon, J. G. and White, H. (1985). Some heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimators with improved finite sample properties. Journal of Econometrics, 29(3), 305–325.

Liang, K.-Y. and Zeger, S. L. (1986). Longitudinal data analysis using generalized linear models. Biometrika, 73(1), 13–22.

See also

frequentist_vcov(), which takes the object.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(150))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(150, sd = 0.2 + dd$x)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, vcov_type = frequentist_vcov())))
#>    mu:(Intercept)              mu:x sigma:(Intercept) 
#>        0.13312662        0.23015913        0.05812382 
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, vcov_type = frequentist_vcov(
  sandwich = hc0_sandwich()))))
#>    mu:(Intercept)              mu:x sigma:(Intercept) 
#>        0.09366361        0.23964065        0.06933911 
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, vcov_type = frequentist_vcov(
  sandwich = hc1_sandwich()))))
#>    mu:(Intercept)              mu:x sigma:(Intercept) 
#>        0.09461453        0.24207361        0.07004307 

# observations in clusters
dd$id <- rep(1:30, each = 5)
fit2 <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
vcov(fit2, vcov_type = frequentist_vcov(
  sandwich = hc1_sandwich(cluster = ~ id)), param = "mu")
#>                mu:(Intercept)        mu:x
#> mu:(Intercept)     0.01088101 -0.02516280
#> mu:x              -0.02516280  0.07551173
